strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and presents a simple, training-free two-stage pipeline: greedy k-center selection before LLM prefilling followed by adaptive removal of the remaining visual tokens in later decoder layers.

The empirical coverage is substantial: LLaVA-NeXT 7B and 13B are evaluated on eight image and four video benchmarks. At 10% token retention, ToDRE reports a strong 95.1% normalized image-benchmark performance, exceeding the evaluated alternatives, while also performing well on video tasks.

The paper evaluates actual efficiency rather than relying only on theoretical FLOPs. On an RTX 3090, it reports reduced memory, 1.9x throughput, and up to approximately 2.6x lower aggregate inference time. The component, threshold, and candidate-layer ablations help explain the two stages.
The method is easy to understand, and the visualizations provide an intuitive account of why spatially diverse token retention can be more robust than concentrated attention-based selection.
weaknesses: The central originality claim is insufficiently established. DivPrune [2] is explicitly titled "Diversity-based visual token pruning" and predates this submission, yet it is neither substantively distinguished nor included in the experiments. Stage 2 is also closely related to Visual Token Withdrawal [35]. Thus, the main algorithm appears to combine a standard greedy k-center procedure with an existing withdrawal idea, without a convincing comparison to the closest prior art.

The theoretical justification in Appendix B is invalid. Orthogonality of two subspaces does not imply statistical independence of arbitrary functions of variables in those subspaces. Lemma 1 simply asserts the needed factorization without assumptions such as an appropriate joint distribution; consequently, the covariance result and the claim that it validates the two-stage design do not follow.

The claimed architecture-agnostic generality is not adequately supported: both evaluated models are LLaVA-NeXT variants sharing the same architecture and vision encoder. Evaluation on genuinely different LVLM families is needed, particularly because the method assumes access to a vision-encoder CLS token and decoder attention matrices.

Important implementation and reproducibility details are missing. The paper does not explain how full cross-modal attention ratios are obtained while retaining claimed compatibility with efficient attention operators such as FlashAttention, whether similarity-search and attention-extraction overheads are included in FLOPs, what happens if no candidate layer meets the threshold, or the normalization required for Algorithm 1 to implement cosine similarity.

Several quantitative inconsistencies reduce confidence. Table 3 labels the reduction from 31.4T to 8.2T as 78.0%, although it is approximately 73.9%. The discussion of Table 4 cites 30:38 to 29:51 for the 25% setting, whereas the table reports 44:40 to 43:09; 29:51 does not appear in the table. The computational analysis also writes encoding and prefilling with the same formula and variables despite their different model dimensions.

The long-generation advantage is asserted but supported only by one qualitative example. Most timing and accuracy results concern short-answer tasks, for which Stage 2 gives only a small incremental speedup over Stage 1. Quantitative evaluation of latency as output length increases is needed to substantiate a major motivation for the second stage.

The baseline protocol is not fully convincing: FastV and SparseVLM are omitted from the 13B study based on claimed degradation without reporting those results, and statistical variation or repeated-run uncertainty is absent. The limitations discussion also does not address the method's potential failure on fine-grained/OCR questions where spatially diverse tokens may omit small task-relevant evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing the substantial inference cost caused by visual tokens in large vision-language models. The proposed training-free pipeline is simple and potentially useful.

Combining early diversity-based selection with later removal of visual tokens is intuitively reasonable. The end-to-end measurements indicate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, including a reduction from 77:04 to 29:31 at 10% retention and competitive memory and throughput results on an RTX 3090.
The empirical evaluation covers eight image and four video benchmarks, two LLaVA-NeXT model sizes, multiple retention ratios, and ablations of both stages, the threshold, and candidate layers.
The paper is generally well organized, and the diagrams and qualitative token-selection visualizations make the approach easy to understand.
weaknesses: There is a fundamental problem with the cross-modal attention formulation. With the stated token order—system, visual, then text—and a causal LLM decoder, visual queries cannot attend to later text keys. Therefore the visual-to-text quantity in Eq. (7) should be identically zero, yet Figure 2 reports large nonzero values and uses this quantity to motivate and trigger Stage 2. The paper must clarify its masking, token ordering, or attention direction; as written, a central observation and part of the algorithm are inconsistent with causal self-attention.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix B is invalid. Orthogonality of feature subspaces does not imply statistical independence, but Lemma 1 simply assumes the required factorization. Moreover, the actual model neither enforces nor demonstrates the proposed orthogonal decomposition. Consequently, the claimed proof that intra- and cross-modal redundancy are independent does not support the method.

The originality of Stage 1 is insufficiently established. It applies the classical greedy k-center algorithm, while the manuscript cites DivPrune [2], whose stated subject is diversity-based visual-token pruning, but neither discusses it substantively nor includes it in comparisons. Stage 2 is also closely related to the cited visual-token-withdrawal approach. The novelty of the combination may have value, but the paper does not convincingly distinguish itself from its closest prior work.

The claim of being architecture-agnostic is not adequately supported: all experiments use the same LLaVA-NeXT architecture family, with only 7B and 13B variants. Testing distinct vision encoders, projectors, LLM families, or modern LVLM architectures is necessary to substantiate transferability.

The claimed compatibility with efficient attention operators is questionable and experimentally unsupported. Stage 2 requires explicit attention probabilities at several layers, whereas common FlashAttention interfaces avoid materializing those matrices. The paper provides no implementation explanation or runtime comparison demonstrating that attention extraction preserves the claimed compatibility and speed.

Evidence for efficiency on long-form generation is especially weak. The paper argues that Stage 2 becomes more beneficial as output length grows, but reports throughput only on POPE and offers only one qualitative long-response example. No latency-versus-output-length, decoding throughput, or long-caption generation experiment validates this central motivation.

Experimental reporting has several reliability issues: no uncertainty or repeated-run analysis is provided; excluded 13B baselines are dismissed as suffering substantial degradation without reporting their results; and the Stage-2 ablation covers only four image benchmarks. The text below Table 4 also incorrectly describes the 25% timing change as 30:38 to 29:51, whereas the table reports 44:40 to 43:09.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. Algorithm 1 uses raw dot products despite the method specifying cosine similarity, without stating that features are normalized. The threshold and candidate layers appear tuned on the same benchmarks used for reporting, and code availability, evaluation prompts, decoding settings, timing protocol, and the overhead of extracting attention maps are not sufficiently documented.

The framing overstates task awareness: Stage 2 does not identify and remove individual task-irrelevant visual tokens; it removes every remaining visual token once a global attention threshold is crossed. Given the serious causal-attention inconsistency, invalid theoretical justification, limited novelty comparison, and incomplete systems evidence, the current scientific case favors rejection despite promising empirical results.

strengths: The paper presents a practical Algorithms/General contribution: a training-free two-stage method combining diversity-based k-center token retention with adaptive removal of visual tokens after cross-modal attention has diminished.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering two LLaVA-NeXT model sizes, eight image benchmarks, and four video benchmarks. At 10% token retention, ToDRE preserves 95.1% of aggregate image performance and consistently outperforms the reported pruning baselines.

The efficiency results are compelling: the method reduces measured total inference time from 77:04 to 29:31 in the ablation setting, reaches 2.8 versus 1.5 samples/s on POPE, and lowers peak memory from 15.9 GB to 13.6 GB on an RTX 3090.

Ablations separately evaluate both stages, the cross-modal-attention threshold, and candidate-layer placement. These results support the claim that diversity selection supplies most of the speedup while later visual-token removal offers a smaller complementary gain.

The method is simple, training-free, applicable to images and videos, and addresses an important practical bottleneck in high-resolution LVLM inference. Orthogonality of visual and textual subspaces does not imply the statistical independence asserted in Lemma 1, so the covariance conclusion does not follow. Moreover, projecting a visual vector from an orthogonal visual subspace onto the textual subspace would be zero, making the proposed cross-modal quantity questionable. This theoretical claim should be removed or substantially reformulated, although the empirical method does not depend on it.

Originality relative to the cited DivPrune work is insufficiently established. DivPrune is explicitly described by its title as diversity-based visual-token pruning, yet it is neither discussed in related work nor included in comparisons. The paper should clearly distinguish its Stage 1 selection rule and evaluate against this particularly close prior method.

Backbone diversity is limited: all experiments use the same LLaVA-NeXT architecture with 7B or 13B Vicuna variants. The architecture-agnostic and broad-transferability claims would be stronger with a substantially different LVLM family and vision encoder/projector.

The claim of excellent compatibility with efficient attention operators is not adequately substantiated. Stage 2 requires explicit aggregate attention probabilities at several decoder layers, but the paper does not explain how these are obtained without materializing attention maps or disabling optimized attention kernels, nor does it isolate this overhead.

Evidence for long-response benefits is only qualitative, despite the argument that Stage 2 becomes increasingly valuable as generation length grows. Runtime and quality curves versus output length would directly test this central motivation.

Several reporting details need correction or clarification. The text below Table 4 gives incorrect 25% timing values, the scope and averaging protocol behind total-time measurements are unclear, and no uncertainty or repeated-run variability is reported for timing. The limitations section also omits the restricted backbone evaluation and possible failure cases where late layers still require visual evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and proposes a simple, training-free two-stage pipeline: diversity-based token selection before the LLM followed by removal of visual tokens in later decoder layers.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering four LVLM backbones and twelve image/video benchmarks. On LLaVA-NeXT, ToDRE generally provides a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, retaining 95.0% normalized performance with 10% of visual tokens and outperforming the strongest reported pruning baseline by 1.5 percentage points on average.

The paper reports multiple efficiency measures, including FLOPs, peak memory, throughput, and end-to-end time. The component ablation indicates that Stage 1 supplies most of the acceleration, while Stage 2 gives an additional reduction in runtime.

The method is compatible with multiple input settings, including AnyRes images and video, and the pivot, threshold, and pruning-layer ablations are useful. The presentation and algorithm description are generally clear.
weaknesses: The claimed theoretical proof of orthogonality is invalid. The analysis simply imposes mutually orthogonal visual and textual subspaces, although LVLM projectors are explicitly trained to align the modalities in a shared space. More importantly, orthogonality does not imply the statistical independence asserted in Lemma 1 for arbitrary functions of the same visual variables. Consequently, the covariance factorization and the paper's claim that it proves independence of the two redundancy measures are unsupported.

The Stage 2 attention formulation appears inconsistent with causal decoder attention. With the stated ordering of system, visual, and text tokens, a visual-token query cannot attend to later text tokens, making the defined visual-to-text attention ratio identically zero under the causal mask. The paper does not explain how the nonzero visual-to-text curve is computed, so the central task-relevance criterion is insufficiently specified and one of its two threshold conditions may be vacuous.

The novelty over DivPrune is limited and not isolated adequately. Both methods greedily retain diverse visual tokens; ToDRE changes the diversity objective from nearest-selected-token/min-max selection to cumulative-similarity/max-sum selection and adds late visual-token withdrawal. There is no controlled comparison of these objectives, and the Stage 2 ablation improves normalized performance by only 0.1-0.2 points while providing modest incremental acceleration.

The strongest practical claim—that Stage 2 becomes increasingly valuable for long generations—is not quantitatively tested. The benchmark outputs are mostly short, while the long-response evidence consists of one qualitative example. Latency, memory, and accuracy as functions of output length are needed to establish this claimed advantage.

Evaluation details needed for reproducibility are incomplete, including exact prompts, decoding settings, image-resolution and video-frame policies, attention implementation, threshold-selection protocol, and whether token-selection overhead is included consistently. No uncertainty or repeated-run measurements are reported, despite several claimed gains being small. The threshold and layer appear to be selected and evaluated on the same four benchmarks, creating a risk of test-set tuning.

Cross-backbone results report only ToDRE rather than comparisons with competing pruning methods, so they demonstrate robustness but not superiority beyond LLaVA-NeXT. Likewise, excluded 13B baseline results are described as suffering substantial degradation but are not shown. The headline 2.6x speedup also needs clearer reconciliation with the 1.9x throughput reported in the main efficiency table. Overall, the empirical results are promising, but the incorrect theory and ambiguity in the Stage 2 mechanism tip this Algorithms/General submission slightly toward rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and proposes a simple, training-free two-stage pipeline that can be applied without modifying model weights.
The empirical scope is reasonably broad: experiments cover four LVLM backbones, eight image benchmarks, four video benchmarks, two retention ratios, and both 7B and 13B LLaVA-NeXT variants.

At 10% token retention, the method reports a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off on LLaVA-NeXT-7B: 95.0% normalized performance, 80.9% fewer FLOPs, 14.5% lower peak memory, and 1.9x throughput. The stage-wise ablation also shows that late-layer removal provides a modest additional runtime benefit.

The paper includes comparisons with several relevant training-free baselines, ablations of the pivot, threshold, and removal layer, and useful qualitative visualizations showing broader spatial coverage than attention-based pruning.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is invalid. The supplement simply assumes that visual and textual embeddings occupy orthogonal subspaces, although the evaluated LVLMs impose no such constraint. More seriously, orthogonality of subspaces does not imply statistical independence or the expectation factorization asserted in Lemma 1. Consequently, the claimed proof that intra- and cross-modal redundancy are orthogonal has no valid basis.

The relevance criterion appears inconsistent with causal decoder attention. The paper orders tokens as system, visual, then text and defines visual-to-text attention using visual queries and text keys. Under the causal mask of the evaluated decoder-only LLMs, those later text keys are inaccessible to visual queries, so this quantity should be identically zero. Figure 2 reports large nonzero values without explaining a different mask or attention convention. This undermines the claimed bidirectional criterion and the information-migration analysis motivating Stage 2.

The claimed adaptive layer selection is not adequately specified or demonstrated. The implementation appears to inspect only the fixed layer 7L/8, while the ablation compares other fixed starting layers. The paper does not report how often the threshold fires, the resulting removal-layer distribution, or what happens when it does not fire. Thus it is unclear whether Stage 2 is genuinely adaptive or essentially fixed late-layer pruning.

Novelty is limited. Stage 1 is closely related to the cited DivPrune diversity-selection formulation, differing mainly through a max-sum rule and pivot choice, while Stage 2 builds directly on the cited information-migration idea from VTW. The incremental value of Stage 2 is small: Table 5 shows only 0.1–0.2 percentage-point normalized accuracy changes and roughly 5–8% additional runtime reduction over Stage 1 alone.

Several strong claims exceed the evidence. Cross-backbone experiments on Qwen and InternVL include no competing pruning methods, so they establish compatibility rather than superiority or architecture-agnostic robustness. The promised advantage for long-output generation is supported only by one qualitative example, with no quantitative latency or quality evaluation on long-form generation.

The evidence lacks uncertainty analysis despite several reported margins being very small, such as 0.2 points over DivPrune on the 10% video setting and 0.1 samples/s in throughput. There are no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance analysis, and the normalized average across heterogeneous benchmarks can obscure task-specific regressions.

Reproducibility details are insufficient for a systems-oriented efficiency claim: decoding settings, batch sizes, baseline implementation provenance, measurement protocol, per-sample token allocation, and hardware-software configuration are incomplete. No code or release commitment is stated. Overall, the empirical Stage 1 results are promising, but the false theoretical argument and unresolved causal-attention inconsistency prevent a technically convincing Algorithms/General contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and proposes a simple, training-free two-stage framework: diversity-based token selection before LLM prefilling, followed by removal of visual tokens once cross-modal attention becomes small. The components are intuitive and complementary.

The empirical evaluation is broad for an efficiency paper, covering four LVLM configurations, eight image benchmarks, and four video benchmarks. On LLaVA-NeXT-7B, ToDRE consistently improves the accuracy-retention trade-off over the reported competitors, retaining 98.2% and 95.0% of baseline performance at 25% and 10% token retention, respectively.

The paper reports actual throughput, peak memory, and end-to-end time in addition to FLOPs. At 10% retention, the method reaches 2.9 samples/s versus 1.5 for the uncompressed model, reduces memory by 14.5%, and substantially shortens aggregate evaluation time.

The ablations separately evaluate both stages, pivot selection, pruning depth, and the relevance threshold. They show that Stage 1 provides most of the acceleration while Stage 2 offers a smaller but measurable additional reduction without degrading aggregate accuracy.

The method is clearly presented, and the supplementary pseudocode and qualitative token-selection visualizations make its behavior reasonably easy to understand. The cross-backbone and video results provide encouraging evidence that the main idea is not confined to one image-only architecture.
weaknesses: The theoretical claim is not sound as written. Orthogonality of visual and textual subspaces does not imply statistical independence of the kernel similarity and relevance variables, yet Lemma 1 assumes precisely this factorization without proof. Moreover, the manuscript does not establish that actual LVLM embeddings satisfy the stated orthogonal-subspace constraint. Thus, the claimed proof that diversity and relevance are orthogonal should be removed or substantially revised; fortunately, the empirical method does not depend on it.

The novelty of Stage 1 is incremental relative to DivPrune, which already performs greedy diversity-based token retention. The paper should more precisely distinguish max-sum selection from DivPrune's min-max objective and isolate whether the gains arise from that objective, pivot initialization, implementation details, or the second stage.

The claimed architecture-agnostic and efficient-attention compatibility is insufficiently demonstrated. Stage 2 requires cross-modal attention probabilities, which standard FlashAttention interfaces do not materialize, while architectures lacking a vision [CLS] token fall back to a random pivot. Implementation modifications and their computational cost are not explained.

Cross-model evidence on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL2 compares ToDRE only with each uncompressed model, not with competing pruning methods. Efficiency measurements are limited to LLaVA-NeXT-7B and POPE, and the anticipated advantage for long-form generation is supported only qualitatively rather than with latency-versus-output-length measurements.

The evaluation reports single aggregate results without uncertainty, repeated-run analysis for the random fallback, or sensitivity across task categories. Some exclusions, such as FastV/SparseVLM on the 13B model and SparseVLM on video, are justified only by asserted transferability problems rather than reported numbers.

Several claims are overstated: the selected pruning depth is effectively tuned to 7L/8 rather than convincingly shown to be dynamically discovered, Stage 2 yields only a modest incremental speed gain after Stage 1, and attention magnitude alone does not establish that visual information has been 'absorbed' into text representations. Reproducibility would also benefit from code, exact prompts and decoding settings, software versions, and detailed timing methodology.
